The nation's aviation system is gradually returning to normal after Friday's four-hour
nationwide ground stop of all flights. The Trump administration says the air traffic
control system shut down because of older equipment that became overloaded during a
computer software update. Thousands of flights were cancelled and tens of thousands of passengers
are being impacted with people scrambling to get rental cars to drive to their destinations
or find scarce hotel rooms. Others, including Kate Tuttle, are struggling to find her luggage
as she travels to Knoxville, Tennessee from Syracuse, New York.
They canceled my flight, so there's no kind of picking that one back up. Luckily for me,
I have a friend who lives in Knoxville, so it's four hours. She's driving to get me.
And then we're going to make our meetings tomorrow, at least. If I can find my luggage,
that's the biggest thing now. We don't know where our luggage is.
Many people this morning are sleeping at airports as they await more information from the FAA and
airlines. Meanwhile, professional and college sports leagues and conferences are scrambling
to reschedule hundreds of athletic events this weekend and get the teams and the referees to
their destinations. Mexico's president says a migrant caravan that was headed north has been
disbanded. NPR's Evander Peralto reports President Trump had threatened Mexico with new tariffs.
In a social media post, President Trump warned that "huge caravans of migrants were beginning
their illegal march through Mexico." He said if Mexico didn't stop them, he would double the
tariffs on the country. But the reality is that migration toward the United States is at historic
lows. Mexican President Claudia Shambaugh said her government had disrupted nearly two dozen
migrant caravans since the beginning of Trump's term. And this new one has already dispersed.
Right now, there is no migrant caravan headed north, she says. Migration has been a point of
contention for these two countries. But despite constant threats from Trump, Mexico has dodged
nearly all new tariffs. Adar Peralto, NPR News, Mexico City.
Despite scandals at Nvidia, tech stocks are climbing after a sharp sell-off last week.
NPR's Stephen Besaha reports. Big tech companies have a long way to go to recover from last month's
artificial intelligence sell-off. Shipmaker Intel's stock rose about 5.5 percent this week. But look
back a month and its stock is still down more than 40 percent. The biggest chipmaker in the market,
Nvidia, is still seeing its stock value fall, down about 12 percent this week. After reports,
it's now ousted CEO Jensen Wong had multiple affairs, including with a woman suspected of
being a Chinese spy. Now that drama is spilling into the upper ranks of the Trump administration.
Treasury Secretary Scott Beset blamed the Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick,
for not restricting Nvidia from selling its most advanced chips to China.
Stephen Besaha, NPR News. And from Washington, you're listening to NPR News.
A federal appeals court in New York says the Department of Transportation wrongly withheld
nearly 74 million dollars in highway money from New York State. The dispute centered on New York
State's decision not to revoke nearly 33,000 commercial driver's licenses that the Transportation
Department said were wrongly issued in many cases to immigrants. Microsoft says it's seeking broad
recovery and stability after a global outage of the Outlook email and other applications earlier
this week. Although some messages may be stuck in the queue, NPR's Andrea Shue reports the stoppage
was felt wide and far. No doubt the widespread outage caused real mayhem for many individuals
and workplaces. Hospitals in the UK found themselves dealing with paper records as their
systems became unusable. Congressional staffers scrambled to keep key conversations going.
But for some others, it was a welcome respite. Caroline Burdzik says she was fortunate. The
employment attorney did not have any filing deadlines to meet that day. Without the constant
digging of emails, she had an extremely productive day, focusing on motions and briefs.
Efficiency is a good thing, but I think we need to press pause from time to time and reflect.
For her at least, the outage was both inconvenient and glorious. Andrea Shue, NPR News.
U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland says he will challenge Senator Chuck Schumer for the
Senate Majority Leader's position in Congress next year. Van Hollen gained nationwide attention
when he helped regain the release of Kilmar Abrego-Garcia. I'm Dan Ronan, NPR News.
